title: The environment
hookLine: stewardship, no waste, water as sacred (6:141; 7:31)

cards: Who owns the river at the edge of town? The city that bills you for it? The farm upstream that pumps from it?
The fish? A verse in the Qur'an doesn't settle the paperwork, but it changes the question. Before humans ever appear on the earth in the story, Allah tells the angels what a person will be.

teach.b: In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall translates the announcement like this: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." The Arabic word is khalifah. A viceroy rules, but in someone else's name.
He holds land that isn't his, and he answers for it. So when Muslims speak about the environment, some of them begin here: humans as stewards, not owners. Second, no waste.
In Surah al-An'am there's an almost lush verse about gardens, trellised and untrellised, date palms, olives, pomegranates, crops of every taste.
Eat of the fruit, it says, pay what's due on the day of harvest, and don't be wasteful.

teach.h: EAT AND DRINK, BUT BE NOT PRODIGAL.
teach.b: The instruction comes back in Surah al-A'raf, beside every place of worship: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." Prodigal is an old word for someone who squanders.
Even at a feast, there's a limit. Third, water.

teach.h: PARTNERS IN WATER, PASTURE AND FIRE.
teach.b: In Sunan Abu Dawud the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Shared, not something one person can hoard while others go thirsty.

teach.h: A TREE A BIRD EATS FROM IS CHARITY.
teach.b: And a line in Sahih al-Bukhari: if a Muslim plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts for him as charity. A bird.
Put together, it's a quiet picture of the earth in this tradition: a trust on loan, with others at the table.

how: Muslim environmental groups and preachers often draw on the idea of humans as khalifah, stewards of the earth, and on the Qur'an's warnings against waste, and some mosques run tree-planting days and water-saving drives.

o: the earth as a trust humans hold, without waste, its water shared
the natural world, given to humans to own and use as they like
a modern concern the Qur'an and hadith never speak about

games.q: stewards of the earth — tap the pairs.
p: a viceroy: holds it in another's name
gardens, harvest, and don't be wasteful
eat and drink, but be not prodigal
partners in water, pasture and fire

s: in the Qur'an's story, humans are placed on the earth as its owners
Pickthall's word is viceroy: one who holds and answers for what belongs to another.
a hadith in al-Bukhari counts a tree as charity even when a bird eats from it
a bird, a person or an animal: whoever eats from it, it counts.
the Qur'an's warning against waste applies only in times of shortage
it comes in the middle of plenty, at the harvest and at the feast: eat and drink, but be not prodigal.

games.q: you plant a tree. years later, a bird eats its fruit, not a person. according to the hadith in al-Bukhari, does that count?
o: only if a person eats from it.
yes: it counts for you as charity.
only if you sell the fruit.
games.why: a bird, a person or an animal: whatever eats from it, it counts as charity. the small surprise is the bird.

practice: Walk back through yesterday and count the taps: the shower, the sink while you brushed, the kettle filled too full, the glass poured and left.
Don't scold yourself; just see the water moving through your day, and pick one tap you could turn down.
If you pray, keep the word viceroy in mind, holding something that isn't yours; if you don't, keep the picture of a shared river.

wordCard.voice: The environment. In the Qur'an's picture, the earth is held in trust by a viceroy, eaten from without waste, its water shared. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: one who stands in another's place; Pickthall renders it viceroy in 2:30.

carryVoice: Your line: stewards, not owners. The river was never only yours. Same time tomorrow.
